en: To officially end or cancel a law, treaty, or right
hook: AB-ROGATE: ROGUE action — wiping AWAY a law.
story: Abrogate. For decades, an old university rule locked the women's halls at eight in the evening, while the men's halls had no curfew at all. After months of protests, the syndicate met and formally abrogated the rule; overnight, it ceased to exist. To abrogate is to formally abolish or cancel a law, right, or agreement. In Latin, ab means away and rogare means to propose a law: to repeal it away. Do not confuse it with arrogate, to claim without right. Synonyms: repeal, revoke, annul.

gre.s: The new regime moved swiftly to ____ the treaty its predecessor had signed, declaring that it would no longer be bound by any of its provisions.
gre.clue: would no longer be bound by any of its provisions

example: After seizing power, the military council abrogated the constitution and governed by decree for the next six years.

en: To leave quickly and secretly, often to escape arrest or with stolen money
hook: ABS-COND: ABSent with the CONDominium money.
story: Abscond. For five years, the treasurer of a village savings group in Mymensingh collected deposits from two hundred families. One morning his house was empty and the safe stood open. A bus conductor remembered a man with a heavy bag buying a ticket to the border. He had absconded: left quickly and secretly, taking the money. The word comes from the Latin for to hide away. Prisoners abscond from jail; cashiers abscond with funds. Synonyms: flee, bolt, decamp.

gre.s: Days before the auditors arrived, the firm's accountant chose to ____ with millions in client funds, slipping out of the country under a false name.
gre.clue: slipping out of the country under a false name

example: The tour operator absconded with the deposits of forty pilgrims, leaving them stranded at the airport with worthless tickets.

en: Apt; very appropriate to the situation
hook: APPOSITE: APPROPRIATE and POSITioned just right.
story: Apposite. At a farewell dinner for a retiring headmaster, a former student stood up and quoted Tagore: "Let me not pray to be sheltered from dangers, but to be fearless in facing them." The headmaster had spent forty years teaching children courage. Heads nodded around the room; the quotation was perfectly apposite: apt and exactly suited to the occasion. Apposite sounds like opposite, but it means something close to the reverse: well placed. Synonyms: apt, pertinent, fitting.

gre.s: The speaker's anecdote, though amusing, was hardly ____: it had nothing to do with the budget crisis the committee had gathered to discuss.
gre.clue: it had nothing to do with the budget crisis

example: Nadia closed her history essay with an apposite line from Nazrul that captured the spirit of the independence movement.

en: To attack violently, physically or with criticism
hook: ASSAIL: ASSAULT someone.
story: Assail. When the young cricket captain dropped an easy catch in the final, social media exploded. Thousands of fans assailed him with insults, cartoons, and angry videos. Even former players criticized him on television. He was assailed: attacked violently with criticism. The word can also be physical, as when soldiers assail a fort, or mental, as when doubts assail you at night. Assail and assault come from the same Latin root, meaning to leap upon. Synonyms: attack, besiege, lambaste.

gre.s: Critics were quick to ____ the report, questioning its methods, dismissing its data, and even impugning the integrity of its authors.
gre.clue: even impugning the integrity of its authors

example: Opposition leaders assailed the transport minister after yet another launch capsized on an overcrowded river route.

en: Extremely greedy for money or wealth
hook: AVARICIOUS: 'I've got to have my RICHES!'
story: Avaricious. Every six months, the landlord raised the rent. He charged tenants for pipes he never repaired, kept every security deposit, and once billed a family for the electricity used during a power cut. His bank accounts were full, but he wanted more, always more. The tenants called him a vulture behind his back. Avaricious means extremely greedy for money or wealth. Avarice is a classic villain's sin; in old stories, the greedy man usually loses everything.

gre.s: Far from being generous, the merchant was so ____ that he charged his own relatives interest on every loan.
gre.clue: Far from being generous

example: Avaricious middlemen bought the farmers' rice cheaply at harvest and sold it back to them at double the price months later.

en: To charm or enchant, often in a deceptive way
hook: BE-GUILE: use GUILE (cunning) to charm.
story: Beguile. A smooth talking salesman visited Babu's village, praising every farmer's wisdom, telling funny stories, and promising that his miracle fertiliser would double their harvest. The farmers were charmed and paid in advance. Then he vanished, and the powder turned out to be chalk. He had beguiled them: charmed them in order to deceive. Notice the hidden word guile, meaning cunning. Beguile can also be gentle, as when music beguiles listeners. Synonyms: charm, enchant, dupe.

gre.s: So seductive was the con artist's wit that he could ____ even skeptical investors, who handed over their savings without ever questioning his fraudulent figures.
gre.clue: So seductive was the con artist's wit

example: The travel advertisement beguiled thousands of young men with promises of high wages abroad that never materialized.

en: To polish until shiny; to enhance a reputation
hook: BURNISH: rub until it BURNS bright.
story: Burnish. Every Friday, Grandfather Rahim takes out the old brass lamp his father brought from Murshidabad and rubs it with a soft cloth until it gleams like gold. He burnishes it: polishes it until it shines. Burnish is also used figuratively. A politician who donates to hospitals just before an election is trying to burnish his image, to make his reputation look brighter. Think of rubbing until the metal almost burns with light. Synonyms: polish, shine, enhance.

gre.s: Hoping to ____ her reputation after the scandal, the executive donated generously to local charities and gave interviews emphasizing her humble origins.
gre.clue: donated generously to local charities

example: The coach hoped that a strong tournament in Sylhet would burnish his record before the board reviewed his contract.

en: Courteous and considerate behavior; mutual respect between groups or nations
hook: COMITY looks like COMMUNITY: people living in harmony.
story: Comity. In the old neighbourhood of Lalbagh, Muslim, Hindu, Christian, and Buddhist families have lived side by side for generations. During Eid, Hindu neighbours receive plates of semai. During Puja, Muslim children watch the processions. At Christmas, everyone gets cake. Disagreements are settled over tea. This harmony is called comity: courteous, considerate behaviour and mutual respect between groups or nations. It looks like community, and it describes a community at its best.

gre.s: Despite fierce competition in the market, the two firms maintained a surprising ____, regularly sharing research and referring clients to each other.
gre.clue: regularly sharing research and referring clients to each other

example: Faculty members of rival departments maintained a polite comity, even sharing laboratory equipment during the funding crisis.

en: A person's behavior and manners; the way one carries oneself
hook: DEPORTMENT: how you COMPORT yourself.
story: Deportment. Before Anika's first job interview at a bank in Motijheel, her aunt gave her a lesson. "Sit straight, do not fidget, greet everyone politely, and never check your phone." The interviewers later told her they hired her partly for her deportment: the calm, courteous way she carried herself. Deportment means a person's behavior and manners, especially in public. Old finishing schools taught deportment by making girls walk with books balanced on their heads. Synonyms: bearing, demeanor, conduct.

gre.s: Though the young diplomat's knowledge of policy was impressive, it was his impeccable ____ that won him admirers: he remained courteous and composed even under hostile questioning.
gre.clue: remained courteous and composed even under hostile questioning

example: The old dance teacher judged her students as much on their deportment off the stage as on their footwork.

en: Lacking a plan, purpose, or enthusiasm; jumping randomly from one thing to another
hook: DESULTORY: like a DESERT wanderer with no map, aimlessly drifting.
story: Desultory. Tanvir sat down to study at eight. Ten minutes of vocabulary. Then a cricket highlight. Then two geometry problems. Then his phone. Then a snack. Then a random article about sharks. At midnight he realized he had learned almost nothing. His study session had been desultory: aimless, jumping randomly from one thing to another with no plan or purpose. A desultory conversation drifts without going anywhere. Desultory effort produces desultory results.

gre.s: His research, once focused and rigorous, became ____ in his later years, as he drifted from topic to topic without completing any project.
gre.clue: drifted from topic to topic without completing any project

example: After the power failed, the office staff made desultory attempts at work before giving up and gathering around the tea urn.

en: Quiet and unsure of oneself
hook: DIFFIDENT is the opposite of CONFIDENT.
story: Diffident. Rahim knew the answer to every question in physics class. But when the teacher asked, he looked at his desk. When she called his name, he spoke so softly that nobody heard. He doubted himself constantly, certain that he would be wrong. In the final exam, he scored the highest in the class. He was diffident: shy and lacking confidence. Diffident is the opposite of confident. The GRE loves this contrast, so remember: dif-fident, the opposite of con-fident.

gre.s: Though brilliant, the young researcher was so ____ that she rarely presented her findings, fearing that colleagues would find fault with them.
gre.clue: fearing that colleagues would find fault with them

example: The diffident young poet read her work so quietly at the Ekushey book fair that the back rows strained to hear.

en: Bewildered; completely confused
hook: FLUMMOXED: sounds like your brain just got FLUMMOXED, flopped and mixed.
story: Flummoxed. The first quant question on Tanvir's GRE showed a strange diagram: overlapping circles, a triangle, and an arrow labelled with a letter he had never seen in a math problem. He stared at it for two full minutes without the faintest idea where to begin. He was flummoxed: bewildered, completely confused. Flummoxed is a fun, informal synonym for befuddled and baffled. Even the word sounds like someone tripping over their own thoughts.

gre.s: The detectives were ____ by the case, as every clue seemed to point in a different direction.
gre.clue: every clue seemed to point in a different direction

example: Grandfather was flummoxed by the new smartphone and kept answering video calls with the camera pointed at the ceiling.

en: Excessively talkative, especially about trivial matters
hook: GARRULOUS: sounds like GARGLE-ous, words gargling out nonstop.
story: Garrulous. On the overnight train to Chittagong, Sara wanted to sleep. The man in the next seat had other plans. He told her about his childhood, his three marriages, his diabetes, his opinions on every cricketer since 1990, and the full plot of a film he had seen twenty years ago. At four in the morning he was still talking. He was garrulous: excessively talkative, especially about unimportant things. It is like loquacious, but more annoying.

gre.s: The usually ____ professor, whose lectures often drifted into long anecdotes, was uncharacteristically brief at the ceremony.
gre.clue: whose lectures often drifted into long anecdotes

example: The garrulous rickshaw puller told me his whole family history during the twenty-minute ride to Old Dhaka.

en: A long, loud, aggressive speech; to lecture at length
hook: HARANGUE: HARASS with a long rant.
story: Harangue. Zayan came home with a lower score than expected on his mock test. His visiting uncle sat him down and spoke without pause for forty-five minutes: about discipline, about wasted money, about how in his day students studied by candlelight. Zayan could not say a single word. It was a harangue: a long, loud, aggressive speech. As a verb, to harangue is to lecture someone at length. Synonyms: tirade, diatribe, rant. Compare a gentle talk, which is the opposite.

gre.s: What was billed as a friendly welcome speech turned into a forty-minute ____, as the chairman berated the new employees about laziness and disrespect.
gre.clue: berated the new employees about laziness and disrespect

example: The referee endured a long harangue from the losing captain, who blamed every decision for his team's defeat.

en: To challenge or call into question someone's honesty or integrity
hook: IMPUGN: IM-PUNCH someone's reputation.
story: Impugn. In court, the defence lawyer could not disprove the witness's testimony. So she tried another strategy: she brought up a lie the witness had told twenty years earlier. "If he lied then," she asked the jury, "why should you believe him now?" She was impugning his honesty: calling his integrity into question. To impugn is to attack someone's truthfulness or reputation. A rumour can impugn an innocent person's character.

gre.s: Rather than addressing the substance of the study, critics tried to ____ the researchers' motives, suggesting they had been paid by industry.
gre.clue: suggesting they had been paid by industry

example: The rival scientist impugned her honesty, claiming without evidence that she had altered the data to fit her theory.

en: In an early, unfinished, and still vague state
hook: INCHOATE: like a chick just INCHing out of its egg, not yet formed.
story: Inchoate. At two in the morning, Ishita had half an idea for a startup, something about connecting village farmers directly with city buyers. She scribbled a few words, drew some arrows, and fell asleep. The plan was inchoate: just begun and not fully formed. Say it in-KOH-it. It comes from the Latin for beginning, and despite the sound, it has nothing to do with chaos. An inchoate feeling is one you cannot yet put into words. Synonyms: embryonic, rudimentary, nascent.

gre.s: The committee's proposals remained ____, little more than a list of vague goals that had yet to be developed into any concrete plan.
gre.clue: had yet to be developed into any concrete plan

example: At sixteen, Rafiq had only an inchoate sense that he wanted to build things, long before he chose to study engineering.

en: To flood; to overwhelm with too much of something
hook: INUNDATE: IN + UNDA (wave). Waves pour in.
story: Inundate. Every monsoon, the river near Joya's village rises above its banks and inundates the rice fields: it floods them completely. Only the tops of the banana trees remain visible. The word also has a figurative sense. When Joya posted her free GRE notes online, she was inundated with messages: hundreds of requests arrived, far more than she could ever answer. Unda is Latin for wave: to inundate is to cover with waves. Synonyms: flood, swamp, overwhelm.

gre.s: The monsoon rains that year were heavy enough to ____ the low-lying villages, forcing thousands of families to flee to higher ground with whatever they could carry.
gre.clue: forcing thousands of families to flee to higher ground

example: After the singer posted her email address online, she was inundated with thousands of messages within a single night.

en: Likely to cause resentment or anger; unfairly discriminating
hook: INVIDIOUS: creates ENVY.
story: Invidious. At the team meeting, the manager held up Farhan's report. "Now this is excellent work." Then he held up Kamal's report. "And this is what not to do." In front of everyone. Kamal's face burned. For months afterward, the team was full of resentment and gossip. The comparison had been invidious: unfairly discriminating and likely to cause resentment. Invidious shares a root with envy. Teachers should avoid invidious comparisons between siblings.

gre.s: Teachers are warned against making ____ comparisons between siblings, which can breed lasting resentment within a family.
gre.clue: which can breed lasting resentment

example: The manager found himself in the invidious position of choosing which of two loyal workers would lose their jobs.

en: Talking a lot; very talkative
hook: LOQUACIOUS: 'loqu' means speak, as in eloquent. A loquacious person never stops speaking.
story: Loquacious. Rafi took a rickshaw to the station, a ten-minute ride. In those ten minutes, the driver told him about his village, his daughter's exam results, the price of rice, his opinion of every politician in the country, and a long story about a goat. Rafi said exactly one word: "Okay." The driver was loquacious: talking constantly and easily, sometimes charmingly, sometimes exhaustingly. Loqu means to speak, as in eloquent. The opposite is taciturn.

gre.s: The usually ____ host surprised his guests by sitting in silence for most of the dinner, barely contributing a sentence.
gre.clue: surprised his guests by sitting in silence

example: Our loquacious tour guide in Sonargaon filled every quiet moment with stories about the old merchant houses.

en: A strict disciplinarian who demands complete obedience
hook: MARTINET: named after Colonel MARTINET, a famously strict French drill master.
story: Martinet. Major Haque, the house master at a cadet college, inspects shoes every morning with a ruler. A crooked bed sheet means extra push-ups; a late arrival means no weekend leave. He tolerates no excuses and no questions. Behind his back, the cadets call him a martinet: a strict disciplinarian who demands complete obedience. The word comes from Jean Martinet, a seventeenth-century French army officer famous for harsh drill. Synonyms: disciplinarian, taskmaster, stickler.

gre.s: Former employees describe the chef as a ____ who would dismiss a cook for a single misplaced garnish, yet his kitchen produced some of the finest food in the city.
gre.clue: would dismiss a cook for a single misplaced garnish

example: Our hostel warden in Rajshahi ran the place like a martinet, locking the gates at nine sharp and fining latecomers.

en: So surprised and confused that one is unsure how to react
hook: NON-PLUS: 'no more' to say; you're speechless.
story: Nonplussed. Arif had prepared answers for every possible interview question. Then the interviewer smiled and asked, 'If you were a vegetable, which one would you be, and why?' Arif opened his mouth, closed it, and stared. He was completely nonplussed: so surprised and confused that he did not know how to react. Careful: many people wrongly use it to mean calm and unbothered. The true meaning is bewildered. Non plus is Latin for no more: nothing more to say. Synonyms: baffled, perplexed.

gre.s: The professor, who seemed to have an answer for everything, was utterly ____ by the child's simple question and stood in silence for a full minute.
gre.clue: stood in silence for a full minute

example: The quizmaster was nonplussed when two contestants gave the same wrong answer at exactly the same moment.

en: Deep respect or a gesture expressing it, such as a bow
hook: OBEISANCE: OBEY + bow down.
story: Obeisance. When the old music master entered the room, his students rose, bowed their heads, and touched his feet, the traditional gesture of respect for a guru. He placed a hand on each head in blessing. Later, a visiting foreigner asked what the gesture meant. A student explained: obeisance. Obeisance means deep respect, or a gesture expressing it, such as a bow. Courtiers paid obeisance to the king. Think: obey and bow down.

gre.s: Courtiers were expected to perform elaborate ____ before the emperor, bowing until their foreheads touched the floor.
gre.clue: bowing until their foreheads touched the floor

example: Each morning the young musicians made obeisance to their guru, touching his feet before the lesson began.

en: To remove a need or difficulty; to make unnecessary
hook: OBVIATE: OBVIOUSLY not needed anymore.
story: Obviate. Every month, Rafi's father used to take a day off work to stand in a long bank queue to pay the electricity, gas, and water bills. Then he learned mobile banking. Now he pays everything from his phone in two minutes while drinking tea. The new system obviated the need for the queue: it removed the need entirely. To obviate is to make something unnecessary. A GPS obviates the need for paper maps.

gre.s: The new vaccine, if effective, would ____ the need for the costly and painful treatments currently used to fight the disease.
gre.clue: the need for the costly and painful treatments

example: Online land records could obviate the long queues and bribes that once accompanied every visit to the registry office.

en: Too eager to tell people what to do; intrusively interfering
hook: OFFICIOUS: acts like an OFFICER nobody appointed.
story: Officious. At a government office in Motijheel, one junior clerk would not let anyone pass without checking their forms, even people looking for the toilet. He corrected spelling on documents that were not his job, told visitors where to stand, and lectured an old man about his handwriting. He was officious: too eager to tell people what to do, intrusively interfering. Careful: officious does not mean official. Synonyms: meddlesome, bossy, intrusive.

gre.s: The ____ hall monitor, who had no real authority, nonetheless insisted on inspecting every student's bag and lecturing teachers about punctuality.
gre.clue: who had no real authority, nonetheless insisted on

example: An officious security guard insisted on checking our tickets three times before letting us into the half-empty theater.

en: Harsh public criticism or disgrace
hook: OPPROBRIUM: OPPOSITE of APPROBATION (praise).
story: Opprobrium. After a factory building collapsed and killed hundreds of workers, investigators revealed that its owners had ignored cracks in the walls and forced people to return to work. The public's reaction was furious: protests, angry headlines, international condemnation. The owners could not leave their homes. They faced opprobrium: harsh public criticism and disgrace. Opprobrium is the opposite of approbation, which means approval. Both are formal GRE words.

gre.s: The athlete, once a national hero, faced public ____ after the doping scandal, with sponsors abandoning him and fans burning his jersey.
gre.clue: sponsors abandoning him and fans burning his jersey

example: The company drew international opprobrium after a factory collapse revealed that it had ignored repeated safety warnings.

en: Calm and unemotional; not easily excited
hook: PHLEGMATIC: slow and calm, like thick PHLEGM.
story: Phlegmatic. The cyclone signal rose to number ten, and the coastal shelter was in panic. Children cried and men shouted over each other. Old Abdul the boatman simply sat in a corner, sharing out puffed rice and calmly telling families where to put their things. He was phlegmatic: calm and unemotional, not easily excited. Ancient doctors believed that too much phlegm in the body made a person sluggish and calm. Synonyms: imperturbable, stolid, unflappable.

gre.s: While the other passengers screamed as the plane lurched through the storm, the ____ pilot calmly announced that they would still land on schedule.
gre.clue: calmly announced

example: Even when the stock market crashed, my phlegmatic uncle simply finished his tea and went back to reading the newspaper.

en: Occurring at a favorable time; lucky, as if by divine help
hook: PROVIDENTIAL: as if PROVIDENCE (God) sent it.
story: Providential. Anika's scholarship interview in Dhaka was at nine, and her bus broke down near Tangail at seven. She stood on the highway in despair. Then a car stopped: the driver was a professor heading to the very same university. She reached the hall with ten minutes to spare. The ride was providential: occurring at a favourable time, as if by divine help. Providence means divine care or guidance. Synonyms: fortunate, timely, opportune, heaven-sent. Opposite: ill-timed.

gre.s: The ____ arrival of a rescue ship, just hours before the leaking boat would have sunk, convinced the survivors that fate had intervened on their behalf.
gre.clue: just hours before the leaking boat would have sunk

example: A providential gust of wind blew the fire away from the crowded slum, giving firefighters time to arrive.

en: Good for your health
hook: SALUBRIOUS: SALUTE to health, as in 'salud!'
story: Salubrious. Doctors told Rafi's grandfather that Dhaka's smoky air was ruining his lungs. So the family moved him to a small house in the hills of Sylhet: fresh breezes, clean spring water, quiet nights, and morning walks through the tea gardens. Within months he was breathing easily and walking two kilometres a day. The climate was salubrious: good for health. Think of the toast salud, meaning health. Salubrious food and salubrious habits keep you well.

gre.s: Wealthy Victorians flocked to the seaside resort, convinced that its ____ air could cure everything from asthma to melancholy.
gre.clue: could cure everything from asthma to melancholy

example: Many retired officers settle in the hills of Sreemangal, praising its salubrious climate and quiet tea gardens.

en: Likely to make someone drowsy or dull
hook: SOPORIFIC: SO POOR, a lecture so poor it makes you sleepy.
story: Soporific. Professor Karim taught economics in a slow, flat voice for two straight hours, reading every word directly from his slides. The ceiling fan hummed. The room was warm. Within twenty minutes, half the class was asleep, heads drooping onto notebooks. One student actually snored. His lectures were soporific: tending to make people sleepy. Warm milk is soporific; so are some medicines. Think: so poor a lecture that it puts you to sleep.

gre.s: Even the most enthusiastic students found the lecturer's monotone delivery ____, and many dozed off before the first hour had ended.
gre.clue: many dozed off

example: A heavy lunch of biryani had a soporific effect on the committee, and the afternoon session dragged on in near silence.

en: Depravity; wickedness
hook: TURPITUDE: TURNING PUTRID morally.
story: Turpitude. A respected judge in a small town was found to have taken bribes to free murderers while sending innocent poor men to prison. The public was horrified, not only by the crime but by the deep wickedness behind it. Lawyers called it moral turpitude: depravity, wickedness. In law, moral turpitude means conduct that shocks the conscience. Turpis is Latin for shameful or base. Synonyms: depravity, vileness, iniquity.

gre.s: Voters could forgive the mayor's clumsiness and even occasional dishonesty, but his profiting from child labor exposed a degree of ____ they found unforgivable.
gre.clue: his profiting from child labor

example: Under the club's rules, any member convicted of moral turpitude, such as fraud, loses membership immediately.
